'''Non-commutative cryptography''' is the area of [[cryptology]] where the [[cryptographic primitive]]s, methods and systems are based on [[algebraic structure]]s like [[semigroup]]s, [[Group (mathematics)|group]]s and [[Ring (mathematics)|ring]]s which are [[non-commutative]]. One of the earliest applications of a non-commutative algebraic structure for cryptographic purposes was the use of [[braid group]]s to develop cryptographic protocols. Later several other non-commutative structures like [[Thompson groups]], [[polycyclic group]]s, [[Grigorchuk group]]s, and  [[matrix group]]s have been identified as potential candidates for cryptographic applications. In contrast to non-commutative cryptography, the currently widely used [[public-key cryptosystem]]s like [[RSA (cryptosystem)|RSA cryptosystem]], [[Diffie–Hellman key exchange]] and [[elliptic curve cryptography]] are based on number theory and hence depend on commutative algebraic structures.

Non-commutative cryptographic protocols have been developed for solving various cryptographic problems like [[key exchange]], [[encryption]]-decryption, and [[authentication]]. These protocols are very similar to the corresponding protocols in the commutative case.

==Some non-commutative cryptographic protocols==
In these protocols it would be assumed that ''G'' is a [[non-abelian group|non-abelian]] group. If ''w'' and ''a'' are elements of ''G'' the notation ''w''<sup>''a''</sup> would indicate the element ''a<sup>−1</sup>wa''.

===Protocols for key exchange===

====Protocol due to Ko, Lee, et al.====

The following protocol due to Ko, Lee, et al., establishes a common [[secret key]] ''K'' for [[Alice and Bob]].

#An element ''w'' of ''G'' is published.
#Two [[subgroup]]s ''A'' and ''B'' of ''G'' such that ''ab'' = ''ba'' for all ''a'' in ''A'' and ''b'' in ''B'' are published.
#Alice chooses an element ''a'' from ''A'' and sends ''w<sup>a</sup>'' to Bob. Alice keeps ''a'' private.
#Bob chooses an element ''b'' from ''B'' and sends ''w<sup>b</sup>'' to Alice. Bob keeps ''b'' private.
#Alice computes ''K'' = (''w''<sup>''b''</sup>)<sup>a</sup> = ''w''<sup>''ba''</sup>.
#Bob computes ''K''' = (''w''<sup>''a''</sup>)<sup>''b''</sup>=''w''<sup>''ab''</sup>.
#Since ''ab'' = ''ba'', ''K'' = ''K'''. Alice and Bob share the common secret key ''K''.

====Anshel-Anshel-Goldfeld protocol====
{{main|Anshel-Anshel-Goldfeld key exchange}}
This a key exchange protocol using a non-abelian group ''G''. It  is significant because it does not require two commuting subgroups ''A'' and ''B'' of ''G'' as in the case of the protocol due to Ko, Lee, et al.

#Elements ''a''<sub>1</sub>, ''a''<sub>2</sub>, . . . , ''a''<sub>''k''</sub>, ''b''<sub>1</sub>, ''b''<sub>2</sub>, . . . , ''b''<sub>''m''</sub> from ''G'' are selected and published.
#Alice picks a private ''x'' in  ''G'' as a [[Word (group theory)|word]] in ''a''<sub>1</sub>, ''a''<sub>2</sub>, . . . , ''a''<sub>''k''</sub>; that is, ''x'' = ''x''( ''a''<sub>1</sub>, ''a''<sub>2</sub>, . . . , ''a''<sub>''k''</sub> ).
#Alice sends ''b''<sub>1</sub><sup>''x''</sup>, ''b''<sub>2</sub><sup>''x''</sup>, . . . , ''b''<sub>''m''</sub><sup>''x''</sup> to Bob. 
#Bob picks a private ''y'' in  ''G'' as a [[Word (group theory)|word]] in ''b''<sub>1</sub>, ''b''<sub>2</sub>, . . . , ''b''<sub>''m''</sub>; that is ''y'' = ''y'' ( ''b''<sub>1</sub>, ''b''<sub>2</sub>, . . . , ''b''<sub>''m''</sub> ). 
#Bob sends ''a''<sub>1</sub><sup>''y''</sup>, ''a''<sub>2</sub><sup>''y''</sup>, . . . , ''a''<sub>''k''</sub><sup>''y''</sup> to Alice. 
#Alice and Bob share the common secret key ''K'' = ''x''<sup>−1</sup>''y''<sup>−1</sup>''xy''.
#Alice computes ''x'' ( ''a''<sub>1</sub><sup>''y''</sup>, ''a''<sub>2</sub><sup>''y''</sup>, . . . , ''a''<sub>''k''</sub><sup>''y''</sup> ) = ''y''<sup>−1</sup> ''xy''.  Pre-multiplying it with ''x''<sup>−1</sup>, Alice gets ''K''.
#Bob computes ''y'' ( ''b''<sub>1</sub><sup>''x''</sup>, ''b''<sub>2</sub><sup>''x''</sup>, . . . , ''b''<sub>''m''</sub><sup>''x''</sup>) = ''x''<sup>−1</sup>''yx''.  Pre-multiplying it with ''y''<sup>−1</sup> and then taking the inverse, Bob gets ''K''.

====Stickel's key exchange protocol====

In the original formulation of this  protocol the group used was the group of [[Invertible matrix|invertible matrices]] over a [[finite field]].

#Let ''G'' be a public non-abelian [[finite group]]. 
#Let ''a'', ''b'' be public elements of ''G'' such that ''ab'' ≠ ''ba''. Let the orders of ''a'' and ''b'' be ''N'' and ''M'' respectively.
#Alice chooses two random numbers ''n'' < ''N'' and ''m'' < ''M'' and sends ''u'' = ''a''<sup>''m''</sup>''b''<sup>''n''</sup> to Bob.
#Bob picks two random numbers ''r'' < ''N'' and ''s'' < ''M'' and sends ''v'' = ''a''<sup>''r''</sup>''b''<sup>''s''</sup> to Alice.
#The common key shared by Alice and Bob is ''K'' = ''a''<sup>''m'' + ''r''</sup>''b''<sup>''n'' + ''s''</sup>.
#Alice computes the key by ''K'' = a<sup>''m''</sup>''vb''<sup>''n''</sup>.
#Bob computes the key by ''K'' = ''a''<sup>''r''</sup>''ub''<sup>''s''</sup>.

===Protocols for encryption and decryption===
This protocol describes how to [[encryption|encrypt]] a secret message and then [[Decryption|decrypt]] using a non-commutative group. Let Alice want to send a secret message ''m'' to Bob.

#Let ''G'' be a non-commutative group. Let ''A'' and ''B'' be public subgroups of ''G'' such that ''ab'' = ''ba'' for all ''a'' in ''A'' and ''b'' in ''B''.
#An element ''x'' from ''G'' is chosen and published.
#Bob chooses a secret key ''b'' from ''A'' and publishes ''z'' = ''x''<sup>''b''</sup> as his public key.
#Alice chooses a random ''r'' from ''B'' and computes ''t'' = ''z''<sup>''r''</sup>.
#The encrypted message is ''C'' = (''x''<sup>''r''</sup>, ''H''(''t'') <math>\oplus</math> ''m''), where ''H'' is some [[hash function]] and <math>\oplus</math> denotes the [[XOR]] operation. Alice sends ''C'' to Bob.
#To decrypt ''C'', Bob recovers ''t'' as follows: (''x''<sup>''r''</sup>)<sup>''b''</sup> = ''x''<sup>''rb''</sup> = ''x''<sup>''br''</sup> = (''x''<sup>''b''</sup>)<sup>''r''</sup> = ''z''<sup>''r''</sup> = ''t''. The plain text message send by Alice is ''P'' = ( ''H''(''t'') <math>\oplus</math> ''m'' ) <math>\oplus</math> ''H''(''t'') = ''m''.

===Protocols for authentication===
Let Bob want to check whether the sender of a message is really Alice.

#Let ''G'' be a non-commutative group and let ''A'' and ''B'' be subgroups of ''G'' such that ''ab'' = ''ba'' for all ''a'' in ''A'' and ''b'' in ''B''.
#An element ''w'' from ''G'' is selected and published. 
#Alice chooses a private ''s'' from ''A'' and publishes the pair ( ''w'', ''t'' ) where ''t'' = ''w'' <sup>''s''</sup>.
#Bob chooses an ''r'' from ''B'' and sends a challenge ''w''&prime; = ''w''<sup>''r''</sup> to Alice.
#Alice sends the response ''w''&prime;&prime; = (''w''&prime;)<sup>''s''</sup> to Bob.
#Bob checks if ''w''&prime;&prime; = ''t''<sup>''r''</sup>. If this true, then the identity of Alice is established.

==Security basis of the protocols==
The basis for the security and strength of the various protocols presented above is the difficulty of the following two problems:

*The ''[[conjugacy problem|conjugacy decision problem]]'' (also called the ''conjugacy problem''): Given two elements ''u'' and ''v'' in a group ''G'' determine whether there exists an element ''x'' in ''G'' such that ''v'' = ''u''<sup>''x''</sup>, that is, such that ''v'' = ''x''<sup>−1</sup>  ''ux''.
*The ''conjugacy search problem'': Given two elements ''u'' and ''v'' in a group ''G'' find an element ''x'' in ''G'' such that ''v'' = ''u''<sup>''x''</sup>, that is, such that ''v'' = ''x''<sup>−1</sup>  ''ux''.

If no algorithm is known to solve the conjugacy search problem, then the function ''x'' → ''u''<sup>''x''</sup> can be considered as a [[one-way function]].

==Platform groups==
A non-commutative group that is used in a particular cryptographic protocol is called the platform group of that protocol. Only groups having certain properties can be used as the platform groups for the implementation of non-commutative cryptographic protocols. Let ''G'' be a group suggested as a platform group for a certain non-commutative cryptographic system. The following is a list of the properties expected of ''G''.

#The group ''G'' must be well-known and well-studied.
#The [[Word problem for groups|word problem]] in ''G'' should have a fast  solution by a deterministic algorithm. There should be an efficiently computable "normal form" for elements of ''G''.
#It should be impossible to recover the factors ''x'' and ''y'' from the product ''xy'' in ''G''.
#The number of elements of length ''n'' in ''G'' should grow faster than any polynomial in ''n''. (Here "length ''n''" is the length of a word representing a group element.)

==Examples of platform groups==

===Braid groups===

{{Main|Braid group}}

Let ''n'' be a positive integer. The braid group ''B''<sub>''n''</sub> is a group generated by ''x''<sub>1</sub>, ''x''<sub>2</sub>, . . . , ''x''<sub>''n''&minus;1</sub> having the following presentation:
:<math> B_n = \left\langle x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_{n-1} \big| x_ix_j=x_jx_i \text{ if } |i-j| >1 \text{ and } x_ix_jx_i=x_jx_ix_j \text{ if } |i-j|=1 \right\rangle</math>

===Thompson's group===

{{Main|Thompson groups}}

Thompson's group is an infinite group ''F'' having the following infinite presentation:

:<math> F = \left\langle x_0, x_1, x_2, \ldots \big| x_k^{-1}x_nx_k=x_{n+1} \text{ for } k<n \right\rangle</math>

===Grigorchuk's group===

{{Main|Grigorchuk's group}}

Let ''T'' denote the infinite [[Rooted tree|rooted]] [[binary tree]]. The set ''V'' of vertices is the set of all finite binary sequences. Let ''A''(''T'') denote the set of all automorphisms of ''T''. (An automorphism of ''T'' permutes vertices preserving connectedness.) The Grigorchuk's group Γ is the subgroup of ''A''(''T'') generated by the automorphisms ''a'', ''b'', ''c'', ''d'' defined as follows:

*<math> a(b_1,b_2,\ldots, b_n) = (1-b_1,b_2,\ldots, b_n)</math>
*<math>b(b_1,b_2,\ldots,b_n) = \begin{cases} (b_1, 1-b_2, \ldots, b_n) & \text{ if } b_1=0\\ (b_1, c(b_2,\ldots, b_n))&\text{ if } b_1=1 \end{cases}</math>
*<math>c(b_1,b_2,\ldots,b_n) = \begin{cases} (b_1, 1-b_2, \ldots, b_n) & \text{ if } b_1=0\\ (b_1, d(b_2,\ldots, b_n))&\text{ if } b_1=1 \end{cases}</math>
*<math>d(b_1,b_2,\ldots,b_n) = \begin{cases} (b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_n) & \text{ if } b_1=0\\ (b_1, b(b_2,\ldots, b_n))&\text{ if } b_1=1 \end{cases}</math>

===Artin group===

{{Main|Artin group}}

An Artin group ''A''(Γ) is a group with the following presentation:

:<math> A(\Gamma) = \left\langle a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n | \mu_{ij} = \mu_{ji} \text{ for } 1 \le i < j \le n \right\rangle</math>

where <math>\mu_{ij} = a_ia_ja_i\ldots</math>  (<math>m_{ij}</math> factors) and <math>m_{ij} = m_{ji}</math>.

=== Matrix groups ===
{{Main|Matrix group}}

Let ''F'' be a finite field. Groups of matrices over ''F'' have been used as the platform groups of certain non-commutative cryptographic protocols.
